title: How do you make a message/event consumer safe against at-least-once duplicate delivery (store a `processed_event_id` / inbox table and skip already-processed IDs, use unique DB constraints, or idempotent state transitions) — and why is "do not corrupt state on reprocessing" the real goal rather than literal exactly-once?
shortTitle: How do you make a message/event consumer safe against at-least-once duplicate delivery

s1_definition.profdef: You make a consumer safe against at-least-once duplicate delivery by making processing idempotent: store each processed event id in an inbox table and skip events already present, enforce a unique database constraint on a natural key so a duplicate insert fails atomically, or use idempotent state transitions that are no-ops when the resource is already in the target state. The real goal is not literal exactly-once delivery, which is practically impossible across independent systems, but ensuring that reprocessing the same event never corrupts state, which gives you effectively-once semantics.
s1_definition.analogy: When the back office at National Bank of India gets a "credit Priya 50000" instruction, it first checks a logbook of instruction numbers it has already handled. If this number is in the logbook, it ignores the instruction and moves on, so even if the mail room delivers the same letter twice, Priya is credited only once. The bank does not try to make the postal service magically deliver each letter exactly once; it just makes sure that handling a letter twice has the same effect as handling it once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make the consumer idempotent with an inbox of processed event ids, a unique constraint, or no-op state transitions, because the achievable and correct goal is that reprocessing never corrupts state, not literal exactly-once delivery.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You make a consumer safe against at-least-once duplicate delivery by making processing idempotent: store each processed event id in an inbox table and skip events already present, enforce a unique database constraint on a natural key so a duplicate insert fails atomically, or use idempotent state transitions that are no-ops when the resource is already in the target state. The real goal is not literal exactly-once delivery, which is practically impossible across independent systems, but ensuring that reprocessing the same event never corrupts state, which gives you effectively-once semantics.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When the back office at National Bank of India gets a "credit Priya 50000" instruction, it first checks a logbook of instruction numbers it has already handled. If this number is in the logbook, it ignores the instruction and moves on, so even if the mail room delivers the same letter twice, Priya is credited only once. The bank does not try to make the postal service magically deliver each letter exactly once; it just makes sure that handling a letter twice has the same effect as handling it once.

**One line to remember:** Make the consumer idempotent with an inbox of processed event ids, a unique constraint, or no-op state transitions, because the achievable and correct goal is that reprocessing never corrupts state, not literal exactly-once delivery.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with why exactly-once delivery is the wrong target. Across independent systems, a broker and a consumer, there is always a moment where the consumer has processed a message but its acknowledgment to the broker is lost, so the broker, unable to know the message was handled, redelivers it. You cannot eliminate this without a perfect distributed agreement that the physics of unreliable networks forbids. So brokers offer at-least-once delivery, which guarantees no message is lost but allows duplicates. Chasing literal exactly-once is chasing a mirage; what you can achieve, and what actually matters, is that processing a duplicate has no additional effect, which people call effectively-once or exactly-once processing.

The first technique is the inbox or processed-event table. You keep a table of processed event ids, and before applying an event you check whether its id is already there; if it is, you skip. The crucial detail is that the check and the insert of the id must be atomic and must commit in the same transaction as the business change. If you check, then process, then record the id as separate steps, a crash in between lets a redelivery reprocess. So you do `INSERT INTO inbox(event_id) VALUES(?)` guarded by a unique constraint and, in the same transaction, perform the business update; if the insert fails as a duplicate, you roll back and skip, because someone already processed this event. This single-transaction coupling is what makes it correct under both duplicates and crashes.

The second technique is a unique database constraint on a natural business key, which is often simpler than a separate inbox. If each event produces a record with a naturally unique key, for example a settlement with a unique trade id, you put a unique constraint on that key and let the duplicate insert fail. The database atomically rejects the second one, and you treat the duplicate-key error as "already processed". This is extremely robust because the guarantee lives in the database and needs no extra lookup.

The third technique is idempotent state transitions, which suit events that drive a state machine. If an event means "move this order to SHIPPED", then applying it when the order is already SHIPPED is a no-op, so reprocessing is harmless by construction. You implement this with a conditional update, for example `UPDATE orders SET status='SHIPPED' WHERE id=? AND status='PLACED'`, which affects one row the first time and zero rows on a duplicate, so the duplicate changes nothing. This needs no inbox at all when the domain already has clear states.

Several senior points round this out. Choose the technique by shape: inbox for general side effects, unique constraint for inserts, state transition for state machines, and often a combination. The id you dedupe on must identify the logical event, not the delivery attempt, and it must be stable across redeliveries. Non-database side effects, like sending an email or calling an external API, are harder because you cannot wrap them in the database transaction, so you either make them idempotent downstream, use the inbox to guard them, or accept at-most-once for truly non-idempotent external calls. You should also prune the inbox with a retention window so it does not grow forever, sized to the maximum redelivery horizon. And the same reasoning is why the real engineering statement is "do not corrupt state on reprocessing": it frames the problem around the invariant you can actually guarantee rather than a delivery property you cannot.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A consumer at National Bank of India credited Priya from a `MoneyCredited` event, then the broker redelivered the same event after a lost acknowledgment, and Priya was credited twice. This is exactly why we need an inbox of processed event ids checked and written in the same transaction as the credit.

Problem 2 — A settlement consumer inserted a settlement row per event and a duplicate event created two rows. This is exactly why a unique constraint on the trade id rejects the duplicate atomically.

Problem 3 — An order-status consumer received a duplicate "ship" event. This is exactly why an idempotent conditional transition makes the second delivery a no-op.

Our mini-project builds a safe consumer demonstrating all three. The code defines an `InboxStore` for processed ids, a `BalanceStore` credited idempotently via the inbox, a `SettlementStore` with a unique trade-id guard, an `OrderStore` with a conditional state transition, and a demo that delivers each event twice to prove reprocessing never corrupts state.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: event EVT-1 crediting CUR3001 by 50000 delivered twice; settlement TRD-7 delivered twice; order ORD-9 shipped twice.

Step 1: EVT-1 arrives. The consumer claims the event id in the inbox atomically and, in the same transaction, credits Priya from 250000 to 300000. The inbox now contains EVT-1.

Step 2: EVT-1 is redelivered. The inbox claim fails because EVT-1 is already present, so the consumer skips the credit entirely. Priya's balance stays at 300000, so the duplicate did not corrupt state.

Step 3: Settlement TRD-7 arrives and inserts a row because the trade id is new. The redelivered TRD-7 fails the unique trade-id constraint, so it is rejected and no second row is created; the row count stays at one.

Step 4: Order ORD-9 is placed, then a ship event transitions it from PLACED to SHIPPED. The duplicate ship event finds the status already SHIPPED, so the conditional transition is a no-op and the status is unchanged.

Step 5: Across all three techniques, the second delivery of each event produced no additional effect, which is the real goal: reprocessing never corrupted state, delivering effectively-once semantics without ever requiring literal exactly-once delivery.

```
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    Credited CUR3001 Rs.50000 from EVT-1
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    DUPLICATE EVT-1 skipped (already in inbox)
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    CUR3001 after duplicate credit = Rs.300000
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    Settle TRD-7: SETTLED
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    Settle TRD-7 again: DUPLICATE (unique trade_id) skipped
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    Settlement rows = 1
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    Ship ORD-9: SHIPPED (applied or already)
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    Ship ORD-9 again: SHIPPED (applied or already)
2026-10-24 14:24:05 INFO    ORD-9 final status = SHIPPED
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  At-least-once delivery → every event may arrive 2+ times
    │
    ├── Inbox technique (general side effect) ──
    │   EVT-1 → claim inbox (TRUE) + credit  ──▶ 300,000   [same transaction]
    │   EVT-1 dup → claim inbox (FALSE) → skip ──▶ 300,000  ✓ no corruption
    │
    ├── Unique constraint technique (insert) ──
    │   TRD-7 → INSERT ok → SETTLED (1 row)
    │   TRD-7 dup → UNIQUE violation → rejected (still 1 row) ✓
    │
    └── State transition technique (state machine) ──
        ORD-9 PLACED → ship: PLACED→SHIPPED
        ORD-9 dup ship → already SHIPPED → no-op ✓

  Goal achieved: reprocessing = same state as processing once (effectively-once)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I always begin by reframing the problem, because the framing is the answer. Literal exactly-once delivery is the wrong target: across a broker and a consumer there is always a moment where the consumer has processed a message but its acknowledgment is lost, so the broker cannot know and redelivers, and no amount of engineering removes that without a perfect distributed agreement the physics of unreliable networks forbids. So brokers give at-least-once delivery, which never loses a message but allows duplicates, and the achievable, correct goal is that reprocessing a duplicate has no additional effect. That is why the real engineering statement is do not corrupt state on reprocessing, and people call the result effectively-once.

To achieve that I make the consumer idempotent with one of three techniques chosen by the shape of the work. The inbox technique keeps a table of processed event ids, and before applying an event I atomically claim its id and, in the same transaction as the business change, commit both; if the id is already present I skip. The critical detail is the single transaction, because if I checked, processed, and recorded the id as separate steps, a crash in between would let a redelivery reprocess. The unique-constraint technique puts a unique index on a natural business key, like a trade id, and lets the duplicate insert fail atomically, which is wonderfully robust because the database enforces it with no extra lookup. The state-transition technique suits events that drive a state machine, where I use a conditional update that moves an order from placed to shipped only if it is still placed, so a duplicate affects zero rows and changes nothing.

The senior points I add are that I pick the technique by shape, often combining them, that the id I dedupe on must identify the logical event and be stable across redeliveries rather than identifying the delivery attempt, and that non-database side effects like emails or external API calls are harder because I cannot put them in the database transaction, so I make them idempotent downstream, guard them with the inbox, or accept at-most-once for truly non-idempotent external calls. I also prune the inbox with a retention window sized to the maximum redelivery horizon so it does not grow forever.

On my project at National Bank of India this came straight from incidents. A consumer credited Priya, lost its acknowledgment, and on redelivery credited her twice, so we added an inbox check and the credit committed in the same transaction. A settlement consumer created duplicate rows on a redelivered event, so we added a unique constraint on the trade id. And an order consumer received a duplicate ship event, which we made harmless with a conditional transition. In every case the fix was not to chase exactly-once delivery but to guarantee that handling an event twice left the system in exactly the same state as handling it once.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I make a consumer safe against at-least-once duplicates with an inbox of processed event ids committed in the same transaction as the business change, a unique constraint on a natural key, or an idempotent state transition, because the goal I can actually guarantee, and the one that matters, is that reprocessing never corrupts state, not literal exactly-once delivery.
